concept: Crypto coin selection for grid and DCA strategies
summary: Source-anchored research for Crypto coin selection for grid and DCA strategies. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: The same short-horizon study warns that its 183-pair panel is not 183 independent replications: it reports mean pairwise correlation of 0.40 and an effective count near 2.5. It also states that the original pairs were ranked by volume measured after the sample ended, leaving survivor-tilted membership. (low confidence)

Fidelity’s performance help says a withdrawal is not treated as a decline in return, while reducing the basis used for its return calculation; its money-weighted method still accounts for withdrawal size and timing. This is a product-specific accounting explanation; the same help text retains withdrawal size and timing in the money-weighted return calculation. (low confidence)

The author page explicitly describes the value-weighted and equal-weighted bias estimates as estimates for buy-and-hold portfolios. The weighting scheme is part of the reported result. (low confidence)

Bull Bitcoin reports a historical comparison from January 1, 2016 to May 13, 2025 using weekly and monthly DCA with a minimum one-year holding period. It reports that DCA outperformed lump sum about 17.5% of the time in its analyzed portfolios, with smoother but lower gains. The post identifies market peaks followed by declines as cases where DCA can outperform in its sample. This is the vendor's reported historical result, not a forecast. The dates, frequencies and holding rule are part of its applicability. (low confidence)

Within its firm-reporting scope, the GIPS handbook combines returns on portfolio cash and cash equivalents with returns on the other portfolio assets. It treats allocation to cash as part of strategy implementation and includes cash performance when the firm controls the cash allocation even if it does not choose the specific cash vehicle. As a methodological application, an already funded reserve inside a bot’s measured portfolio should remain in that portfolio’s performance record during idle periods. (low confidence)

IBKR’s combined-component procedure first aggregates daily market values and flows across components, calculates a combined daily return, then geometrically links those daily returns. It states that adding component returns over the period does not produce the combined portfolio return. This is a useful accounting constraint when a study combines several bot sleeves or reserve accounts under one boundary. (low confidence)

For a proposed scheduled-DCA, grid or averaging-down comparison, report the funding boundary and reserve treatment alongside the return definition. TWR seeks to neutralize external flows, while the cash allocation already inside a portfolio remains part of strategy performance; MWR also reflects investor funding timing. Reporting these perspectives together is a methodological application of the distinction between external funding and cash already allocated within the portfolio. (medium confidence)

Bailey and coauthors state that their PBO procedure does not check whether a backtest has correct transaction costs or uses only data available at the decision time. They also warn that it can miss overfitting to a regime when the available dataset contains no structural break outside that regime. (low confidence)

In their 32-series portfolio example, Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin explain that randomly shuffling individual daily returns destroys autocorrelation. They instead use blocks of returns and the same block starting points across series to preserve the cross-market correlation structure. Their example does not supply a universal block length for crypto bot equity. (low confidence)

The cited bot setup guide says Amount per trade applies separately to each selected pair and warns that simultaneous deals can cause insufficient balance. Its Summary-box documentation says bots and pairs compete for the same available funds, so their full requirements must be added. (medium confidence)

Bitsgap says a price-step DCA ladder struggles when price grinds downward without a meaningful bounce, because every safety order can fill and the ladder runs out. Block Research describes the same path as locking capital in unrealized drawdown after the last safety order. (medium confidence)

The term Amount per trade has different meanings in the cited vendor guides: the cited bot setup guide defines it as the initial position size, while Cornix defines Amount Per Trade as the total potential amount assigned to a complete DCA cycle. (medium confidence)

Cornix states that Stop Loss Timeout can delay closure after the stop price is reached. It separately documents a continuous-stop count to deactivate the bot, a cooldown after trade close, and a total-cycle count before manual reactivation. (low confidence)

OKX distinguishes nominal leverage from effective leverage: increasing position value without increasing margin raises effective leverage even if the nominal setting stays fixed. Its estimated-liquidation calculation assumes orders fill sequentially and stops if the liquidation price rises above the next execution price, so that estimate does not assume the bot can always reach every remaining safety order. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Binance's Futures Grid FAQ gives a fee-adjusted geometric profit-per-grid formula and warns when profit per grid may not cover trading fees. The Dynamic Grid Trading paper uses a transaction fee of 0.0008 and reports lower profits from small grid sizes because fees consume a larger share of arbitrage profit; it also attributes poor IRR at large grid settings to infrequent activation. These are venue- and study-specific assumptions and findings. (medium confidence)

Bybit's spot-grid documentation distinguishes realized Grid Profit from Total P&L, which includes unrealized changes in the held base token. It explicitly states that Grid Profit can remain positive while Total P&L is negative when inventory losses exceed realized profits. (medium confidence)

Lipton and Lopez de Prado's abstract models oscillation using an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and describes exits at a profit target, a maximum tolerated loss or a maximum holding horizon. It develops an analytical framework for profit-taking and stop-out levels by maximizing Sharpe ratio in that model. Leung and Li's abstract separately includes a stop-loss constraint in optimal entry and exit analysis. (medium confidence)
With the same cash amount invested at each interval, scheduled DCA buys more units when price is lower and fewer units when price is higher. (medium confidence)

When the full investment amount is already available, spreading investment over time retains some cash and can forgo gains from immediate investment. FINRA and Vanguard describe this as an opportunity cost. (medium confidence)
FINRA warns that per-transaction commissions or fees can make scheduled DCA more expensive than lump-sum investment because DCA creates more transactions. (low confidence)

Time-weighted return (TWR) seeks to neutralize external cash-flow timing to evaluate the underlying investment management. Money-weighted return (MWR) reflects the investor’s experience, including the amount and timing of deposits and withdrawals as well as investment performance. The GIPS handbook, Fidelity help and IBKR white paper make this distinction. (high confidence)

The GIPS handbook distinguishes a true TWR calculation, which values the portfolio and calculates return with every external cash flow, from less exact large-flow or day-weighted approaches. IBKR describes breaking the period into sub-periods and geometrically linking their returns; it explicitly warns against simply adding sub-period returns. (medium confidence)

Define the measured portfolio before classifying cash flows. GIPS defines an external flow as cash or investments entering or leaving a portfolio. IBKR separately specifies account-level deposits, withdrawals and position transfers, and symbol/asset-level opening and closing proceeds. Applying those scoped definitions to a bot study requires an explicit account or strategy boundary; a trade inside the chosen portfolio should not automatically be treated as an investor deposit. (medium confidence)

The GIPS handbook defines uncalled committed capital as pledged capital not yet drawn and excludes it from total firm assets because it is not actively under management and may never be called. That scoped rule is different from its treatment of cash already held in a portfolio. A bot study should disclose whether “committed capital” means funded portfolio cash, a future contribution plan, or an undrawn pledge before applying either treatment. (low confidence)

For the handbook’s daily-weighted external-flow approximation to TWR, external flows are weighted by the days they were in the portfolio and available for investment. Its Modified Dietz discussion likewise weights each flow by time held. This supports recording when funding becomes available; it does not support counting every later contribution as though it had been present for the entire test. (low confidence)

IBKR describes Modified Dietz as a cash-flow-weighted portfolio-return calculation with a computational advantage over IRR, since it does not require iterative solving. The GIPS handbook calls Modified Dietz an estimate of TWR in its daily-weighted-flow context and distinguishes it from true flow-by-flow TWR. Report the actual algorithm and linking convention; a provider’s MWR or TWR label does not make Modified Dietz an exact IRR or a true flow-by-flow TWR. (medium confidence)

The GIPS handbook says Modified Dietz avoids valuation on every external-flow date but is less accurate than valuing at each flow. Its estimate suffers most when large external flows coincide with high market volatility and significantly non-linear portfolio returns. As a methodological application, the approximation needs explicit scrutiny when a repeatedly funded bot test combines large external flows with volatile, non-linear returns. (low confidence)

More frequent valuation is not sufficient if marks are wrong. The GIPS handbook warns that inaccurate sub-period investment prices can create larger errors than midpoint or day-weighted approximations, and that compounding will not automatically fix mispricings or improperly booked transactions when external flows occur. (low confidence)

Interactive Brokers explains that money-weighted return gives greater weight to performance when the portfolio is larger. Its example describes good performance on a small portfolio followed by a deposit and adverse market performance. Time-weighted return instead isolates the rate from when funds are added or removed. As a methodological application, the size and timing of funding belong in the explanation of differing investor-return assessments. (low confidence)

The GIPS Firms Handbook cautions that an internal-rate-of-return calculation can have multiple answers when both positive and negative external cash flows occur. A reported rate therefore should not be presumed unique merely because a solver returned a value. (low confidence)

For pooled-fund reporting, the GIPS Firms Handbook warns against directly comparing a time-weighted index return with a since-inception money-weighted return. It describes a public-market-equivalent comparison that reproduces the fund’s cash flows using a total-return index. As a methodological application, a cash-flowing bot study should align the benchmark’s return convention and cash-flow history with the portfolio return being compared. (low confidence)

Bailey and coauthors explain that testing many configurations on the same historical data increases the probability of finding false positives. A significance level for one test does not control the selection process across many tests. (low confidence)

Bailey and coauthors describe overfitting as the case in which the configuration with maximum in-sample performance systematically underperforms other configurations out of sample because it has fitted training noise. (low confidence)

Bailey and coauthors explicitly warn against using PBO as the objective function for selecting an optimal strategy. They present CSCV as an assessment of the strategy-selection process and call using it to guide the optimal-strategy search a misuse. (low confidence)

Two Binance Square community posts give different profit-per-grid rules of thumb: one suggests roughly 0.4% after fees, while another recommends net return per grid between 0.5% and 2%. These are attributed recommendations. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

The Short-horizon mean reversion study reports significant directional reversal in 90% of 183 Binance pairs and a gross edge peaking near 1.3 bp per trade against a 5 bp benchmark round-trip cost. The reported experiment evaluates directional sign predictability, and its authors distinguish detectability from profitability at that benchmark cost. (low confidence)

The Dynamic Grid Trading paper reports BTC and ETH backtests from January 2021 to July 2024 and attributes much of its reported peak 60–70% IRR performance to rising cryptocurrency prices. A Stevens Institute project separately reports that its machine-learning parameter variants did not outperform traditional grid methods. These are reported study results. (medium confidence)

Bybit's Spot Grid FAQ states that initialization fails when estimated fill price deviates more than 10% from current market price, with the investment credited back. It separately describes failed initialization when slippage on the initial market buy leaves insufficient arbitrage opportunity or insufficient quote token to place the required orders. This is a venue-specific initialization safeguard. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

The SSRN abstract and author page for Ammann, Burdorf, Liebi and Stöckl's Survivorship and Delisting Bias in Cryptocurrency Markets report a sample of 3,904 cryptocurrencies from 2014–2021 and estimated annualized bias of 0.93% for value-weighted portfolios and 62.19% for equal-weighted portfolios. The two pages describe the same study. (low confidence)

Cong, Li, Tang and Yang's NBER working paper tests 29 exchanges using data from July to November 2019 and estimates wash trading averaged over 70% of reported volume on the unregulated exchanges in its sample. Separately, Coin Metrics describes a Trusted Exchange Framework that vets data quality before calculating market metrics and selecting index constituents. (medium confidence)

CoinMarketCap describes its Liquidity Score as simulated immediate buy and sell slippage over order sizes from about $100 to $200,000, with greater weight on $100–$10,000 orders. S&P Global separately evaluates market volume, bid-ask spread, depth and slippage, and its report table gives mean 1% total Binance depth of EUR 0.40 million for EUR-USDC, EUR 1.00 million for BTC-EUR and EUR 31.10 million for BTC-USDT. These figures describe that report's sample. (medium confidence)

CoinMarketCap describes its Liquidity Score as a purely quantitative measure using exchange API order books or exchange submissions, refreshed every two hours subject to order-book data availability. S&P separately describes cumulative bid-side and ask-side depth for a specified date and reports few executable Kraken USDC-USD trades within 1% of the peg in its March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank crisis example; it says participants might have been more willing to buy larger orders at the 10% level. These are provider descriptions and report examples. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Wash-trading estimates in the reviewed sources depend on estimator and coverage. Cong, Li, Tang and Yang report over 70% for their main unregulated-exchange estimate, about 61% after exchange-characteristic controls, and 16.3 percent for an alternative Benford-based estimate; they explain that the Benford method misses some wash trading. Coin Metrics calls Trusted Volume a lower-bound estimate that excludes DEXes and uncovered centralized exchanges, and warns that calculating an overall fake-volume percentage can give misleading conclusions. (medium confidence)

Vanguard's illustrated historical comparison reports lump-sum outperformance in 68% of rolling one-year periods. That example compares immediate investment with three equal monthly investments, assumes an equity portfolio with no interest on uninvested cash, and uses MSCI World Index returns from 1976–2022. (low confidence)

After price falls beyond the deepest safety order, the cited Summary-box documentation says the bot has spent its safety orders, holds the position, and cannot improve the average with further safety orders. (low confidence)

OKX states that a futures DCA position may be liquidated if its margin balance falls below maintenance margin and that this can lose the initial funds. Bitsgap also distinguishes futures DCA liquidation risk from its spot DCA description. (medium confidence)

The cited the cited bot setup guide setup guide says Max Open Positions limits the cumulative number of open strategies across DCA bots and ignores or cancels new trade signals until an existing strategy closes when that limit is reached. (low confidence)

KuCoin warns that low liquidity can cause large slippage and a situation where a trader can buy but cannot sell. A Binance Square community guide similarly warns that thinly traded coins can gap through several grid lines at once. (medium confidence)

Binance's Futures Grid FAQ states that grid price differences cannot be below tick size and that each grid order must meet a minimum notional requirement. A Binance Square spot-grid guide separately notes that every grid line must meet the pair's minimum order size. These constraints depend on venue and product. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Binance's Futures Grid FAQ includes realized profit, unrealized PnL and funding fees in total profit. A Binance Square futures-grid guide lists funding fees among contract-selection considerations and warns that leverage amplifies losses and can increase liquidation risk. These are futures-grid considerations. (medium confidence)

OKX's Spot Grid documentation states that Trailing Down can extend the lower grid boundary when price continues falling. Each extension requires additional main-account capital; if funds are insufficient, the grid does not extend further. Its risk description warns of over-accumulating during a long bear market. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

The abstract of the preprint Volatility Harvesting or Inventory Risk? reports positive average after-cost grid increments at three- and five-year horizons for Chinese equity ETFs relative to a static portfolio with the same initial exposure. It also reports limited historical signals and no stable out-of-sample spacing-selection advantage over fixed rules. These are abstract-reported results for equity ETFs. (low confidence)

The HODL Strategy or Fantasy? abstract reports Monte Carlo simulations across 378 non-stablecoin crypto assets, net of trading fees and the opportunity cost of one-month Treasury bills. It reports a median excess return of -28.4 percent at a two-to-three-year horizon. Its separate prediction analysis reports economically negligible and unstable effects from endogenous predictors based on realized risk-return metrics. These are the paper's reported simulation and prediction results. (low confidence)

The same study's SSRN abstract reports that a survival-conditioned sample overestimates its size premium by 50%. After controlling for survivorship and delisting bias, the abstract reports no evidence of a positive relationship between average returns and one-week momentum, market beta or downside risk. (low confidence)

Concretum's tutorial describes using CoinMarketCap's historical OHLCV endpoint to retrieve daily open, high, low, close, volume and market cap by numeric coin ID. It presents a download workflow including active and defunct projects and warns that full execution can exceed 20 hours because of rate limits. These are the tutorial's stated data fields and execution warning. (low confidence)

Cong, Li, Tang and Yang limit their wash-trading transaction sample to BTC, ETH, XRP and LTC, and the paper treats cryptocurrency-USD and cryptocurrency-USDT pairs as the same. Those are explicit sample and quote-currency conventions of this study. (low confidence)
FINRA explains that gradual investment can limit losses during a significant decline because cash that has not yet been invested is unaffected by that decline. (low confidence)

Fidelity's crypto-DCA guidance states that the strategy does not assure profit or protect against losses in declining markets and may involve long periods below cost. It cautions that many smaller cryptocurrencies have not made new highs in each market cycle and asks investors to consider their ability to continue purchases during low-price periods. These are the provider's risk warnings. (low confidence)

MarketVector compares a 52-week Bitcoin DCA schedule with immediate lump sum for historical entry days at least 50% below the prior high, using 2013–2023 data. It reports one-year median returns of +50% for DCA and +99% for lump sum in that selected set. It separately reports negative one-year median returns for both strategies at the first 50% breach. The article states that its six completed bear episodes are small in statistical terms and that past recovery patterns cannot be assumed to repeat. (low confidence)

Sato's investment-timing paper defines effective exposure as time-integrated invested capital and distinguishes expectation-level risk from dispersion of realized outcomes. Under stationary finite-variance returns, it compares timing schedules on an exposure-normalized basis and concludes that no simple dominance relation follows once exposure profiles and uncertainty are considered. This describes that paper's probabilistic framework. (low confidence)

O’Brien and Piros's equity-allocation model assumes momentum, reversion and transient mispricing. Their abstract reports scenarios in which typical risk-averse investors prefer DCA to immediate investment in an optimal buy-and-hold allocation. The paper contrasts this equity-model result with the traditional random-walk model. (low confidence)

A Journal of Risk and Financial Management study compares staged and immediate investment across inflation regimes using United States stock and Treasury data. Its abstract reports higher average real terminal wealth from DCA in high-inflation windows, statistically significant for Treasuries but not the S&P 500, and significant lump-sum outperformance in low-inflation windows. These are conditional non-crypto results. (low confidence)

The cited Bitcoin buying guide’s permutation example reports unchanged coin count and average cost after reordering the same purchase prices and then describes DCA as removing sequence risk. Kitces separately states that sequence-of-return risk applies to accumulators contributing cash to a portfolio. The two sources frame the outcome differently; the fixed-purchase-price example concerns units and average cost. (medium confidence)

Interactive Brokers states that time-weighted return removes cash-flow timing effects while leaving market effects and portfolio-manager actions. Removing external-flow timing therefore must not be represented as removing market effects or demonstrating risk-adjusted skill. (low confidence)

The cited bot setup guide allows take-profit to use either the initial order or the average position price. A basket target tied to average entry is therefore a configuration choice in that guide, rather than a universal property of every DCA bot. (low confidence)

The cited Summary-box documentation defines maximum price drop covered as the deviation of the final safety order. Its cumulative-step formula is deviation(k) = p x (c^k - 1) / (c - 1) when c differs from 1, and p x k when c equals 1. (low confidence)

The cited Summary-box documentation defines required capital as the base order plus every safety order. For a safety-order volume multiplier m that differs from 1, it gives Required = V0 + V1 x (m^n - 1) / (m - 1). (low confidence)

Bitsgap warns that weak liquidity and wide spreads can consume the small take-profit targets used by its DCA bot. This is a vendor description of execution risk, rather than independent evidence of a profitable coin-selection threshold. (low confidence)

Bitsgap describes averaging down as lowering average entry while adding exposure during a continued decline, and says it does not protect against a market that keeps falling. Block Research explicitly calls buying more as price drops a mechanic rather than an edge. These are scoped descriptions and commentary, rather than a measured positive expected-return result for the ladder itself. (medium confidence)

KuCoin's spot-grid documentation prefers liquid pairs with two-sided price movement and explains that a one-sided market may keep buying or selling instead of completing repeated buy-low/sell-high cycles. Bitsgap likewise describes frequent swings within a range as suitable and persistent one-way movement as unsuitable. (high confidence)

KuCoin's guidance prefers high liquidity and high volatility, whereas HaasOnline describes moderate volatility as suitable and advises avoiding volatility spikes. Bybit describes the tradeoff: wider swings can complete more grid trades, but swings large enough to exit the range halt execution. These are attributed qualitative guidelines. (medium confidence)

Passivbot documents unilateralness as the absolute ratio of the exponential mean of completed one-minute log returns to the square root of their exponential mean square. It calls this directionality rather than absolute move magnitude. The documentation says implementation tests establish semantics and disabled-feature parity rather than profitability, and recommends assessing drawdown, exposure, underwater time, missed recoveries, fees and returns rather than fill counts alone. (low confidence)

Concretum's dataset tutorial describes CoinMarketCap's numeric UCID as a persistent identifier rather than a ticker, including across branding changes or delistings. Gimmer separately warns that the same ticker need not identify the same asset or contract and recommends recording venue, base, quote, symbol and listing or removal history. (medium confidence)

For a removed market, Gimmer recommends retaining it through its last eligible timestamp and explicitly stating how an open position is handled, rather than silently deleting that record from the historical test. (low confidence)

Gimmer explicitly advises against treating every delisted asset as a total loss: it distinguishes removal, rename, migration and data loss, and calls for verified market history and an explicit open-position rule rather than assigning zero value or a successful exit without evidence. (low confidence)

A comparison of investing an already-available lump sum with investing it gradually differs from investing income as it becomes available. FINRA says the held-cash opportunity-cost argument does not apply to paycheck contributions invested as earned, and Vanguard explicitly distinguishes its lump-sum question from investing a fixed amount from each paycheck. (medium confidence)

In the GIPS handbook, IRR is a commonly used method for MWR, defined in prose as the rate equating present values of inflows and outflows. An MWR calculated by IRR uses a single IRR over the measured period, rather than linking sub-period IRRs. Fidelity’s performance help also describes its personal money-weighted return as an internal rate of return. This does not make every reported MWR an exact IRR calculation. (medium confidence)

The GIPS handbook defines fair value using an orderly arm’s-length sale between willing parties, prioritizes an observable unadjusted quote for an identical investment in an active market when available, and includes accrued income. This is scoped valuation guidance for marking held assets; a bot comparison still needs an explicit inventory-pricing policy rather than substituting only closed-trade proceeds for portfolio valuation. (low confidence)

The GIPS handbook allows beginning-of-day or end-of-day external-flow assumptions but emphasizes establishing and consistently applying the policy. IBKR’s white paper states its own account-level end-of-day assumption. A bot evaluator should disclose the chosen flow-timing convention instead of silently treating one provider’s convention as universal. (medium confidence)

The GIPS Firms Handbook explains why client-driven external flows motivate time-weighted manager comparisons, but also recognizes strategies in which manager-controlled flow timing is part of the investment decision. In its reporting framework, permission to present money-weighted returns instead of time-weighted returns requires both control over external flows and specified portfolio characteristics; control alone is not the entire test. (low confidence)

Quantpedia's grid examples show that a strategy can have losing days when price trends within the day instead of oscillating. Its comparison is an illustrative currency-grid study, rather than evidence ranking present-day crypto coins. (low confidence)

Freqtrade documents a per-pair profit-to-drawdown objective that returns the worst pair's result so that strong pairs do not conceal weak pairs. This documents an available objective, rather than evidence that it improves a grid or DCA coin-ranking strategy. (low confidence)

Freqtrade documents Calmar and profit-versus-drawdown optimization objectives. Their availability shows that maximizing profit and controlling drawdown are distinct configurable objectives; it does not determine the best weights for a candidate-coin ranking. (low confidence)

Freqtrade's documentation warns that increasing optimization precision beyond its default three decimal places will usually produce overfitted results. This is a tool-specific warning about search complexity, rather than a universal parameter-precision rule. (low confidence)

Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin argue that optimization using maximum drawdown may have significant statistical error because the decision rests on one observation of maximal loss. This is their stated limitation of the criterion, rather than a measured uncertainty interval for crypto grid/DCA rankings. (low confidence)

The pinned Frontiers crypto-microstructure study states that it standardizes test features with training-set statistics, right-aligns rolling features so they exclude the forecast interval, and applies its purged walk-forward scheme to hyperparameter tuning and stability selection. These are reported leakage controls for that study, rather than validation of a grid/DCA rolling asset-selection rule. (low confidence)

In its five-minute long/short experiment aggregated over twelve crypto asset-venue pairs, the pinned Frontiers study reports that all net Sharpe ratios are deeply negative after its Binance VIP-0 fee and slippage assumptions. The authors describe the result as diagnostic rather than prescriptive. This is a negative result for that short-horizon experiment and does not show that grid/DCA ranking fails or succeeds. (low confidence)

Vanguard explicitly distinguishes investing a lump sum that is available immediately from investing a fixed amount from each paycheck. In its historical lump-sum versus cost-averaging comparison, the base illustration assumes no interest on uninvested cash; its cash-interest sensitivity says that higher cash interest reduces the lump-sum advantage, all else equal. These are benchmark assumptions in a stock/bond study and do not establish a crypto coin-ranking advantage. (low confidence)

Bailey and coauthors describe a partition-size trade-off in CSCV: too few partitions underrepresent the left tail of the logit distribution, while too many can break relevant temporal and seasonal structure across partitions. This is a property of their validation construction, rather than an established training-window or rebalance rule for crypto grid/DCA selection. (low confidence)

Vanguard illustrates lump-sum versus cost-averaging outcomes using a common initial wealth of $100,000 and a one-year evaluation horizon, with the cost-averaging investment split into three equal monthly parts. These are explicit assumptions of a stock/bond allocation comparison, rather than a crypto coin-selection result. (low confidence)

Bitsgap describes its price-step DCA bot as a base order followed by lower safety orders and a whole-position take-profit above the average entry. Block Research distinguishes this price-triggered averaging-down from time-based DCA at a fixed interval. (medium confidence)

The cited Summary-box documentation recommends leaving available-balance headroom for fees, slippage and other bots. It states that its summary figures assume all safety orders fill and exclude fees and slippage. (low confidence)

Bitsgap describes pullbacks followed by partial recoveries as the favorable path for its DCA bot. It says a straight upward move after the base order leaves only that small initial buy in the trade. (low confidence)

OKX warns that a martingale strategy can increase spending rapidly after a few transactions, especially during a prolonged price decline, and that exiting after funds run out can produce high losses. (low confidence)
Both the cited the cited bot setup guide setup guide and the Cornix settings guide allow a stop-loss baseline to use either the initial/first entry or the average entry. (medium confidence)

Bitsgap qualifies its platform profit-rate analysis as pooling real-money and demo bots and removing unfinished launches, small deposits and outliers; it also says the typical size of losses is not published. Separately, Block Research describes frequent small closed wins alongside a large unrealized open loss. These source-specific disclosures show why a closed-profit rate alone does not quantify whole-account losses or expected returns. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

The cited the cited bot setup guide setup guide distinguishes Position averaging, which begins applying its order-size multiplier from the second extra order, from Order averaging, which applies it from the first extra order. It also distinguishes fixed coin amount from fixed quote-currency order value. A ladder capital calculation must identify which of these documented configurations it represents. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

OKX documents a configuration-specific exception to an assumed positive liquidation price: for a long Futures DCA position, an absent estimated liquidation price may mean its margin is sufficient that it would not liquidate even at a zero asset price. The documentation uses "may"; absence of the displayed price alone is not an unconditional safety guarantee. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Stopping new activity need not release an existing position: the cited bot setup guide documents a Stop choice that leaves trades open and monitored, while OKX says pausing its Futures DCA bot cancels pending orders but retains the current position and keeps TP/SL active. These documented controls therefore require an explicit distinction between pausing new orders and closing inventory. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

The Dynamic Grid Trading paper concludes that its finite grid has zero expected value under its stated equal-probability up/down price-step model, with no transaction fees and liquidation below the lower grid boundary. This is a conditional model result. (low confidence)

KuCoin's example stops buying below the lower grid boundary and stops selling above the upper boundary. The Dynamic Grid Trading paper's reset variant retains cryptocurrency after a lower-bound break and uses arbitrage profits as principal for a new grid. The descriptions use different boundary rules. Bitsgap warns that a grid in a strong uptrend can sell too early and miss the continuation. (medium confidence)

Bitsgap publishes a rule of thumb to inspect the last 30–60 days for a recognizable price range before launching a grid bot. A Binance Square guide describes AI settings that select a range and grid count from recent price history. These are setup heuristics described by the authors. (medium confidence)

Passivbot's Forager documentation describes volume pruning followed by weighted ranking using quote volume, EMA entry readiness, volatility measured by a one-minute EMA of ln(high / low), and an optional unilateralness penalty for sustained one-way movement. Its configuration reference separately documents volume and volatility EMA inputs and score weights. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Martin and Schöneborn's abstract describes a no-trade buffer under linear transaction costs and a low-cost cube-root relation for its width. Leung and Li's abstract derives entry and exit intervals for an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck spread subject to transaction costs, with a stop-loss extension. These are results for their models. (medium confidence)
KuCoin states that USDT/USDC price fluctuations are small and therefore grid profits on that pair will be low. This is the exchange's description of a low-fluctuation pair. (low confidence)

Freqtrade's plugin documentation describes VolatilityFilter as retaining a configured band between minimum and maximum historical volatility. It separately describes RangeStabilityFilter as removing pairs whose historical high-low range lies below or above configured bounds. These are software screening mechanisms. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Coinbase Learn describes grid trading as suitable for both trending and sideways markets. Bybit Learn says strongly one-directional markets are less suitable and describes execution stopping outside the range without an applicable trailing feature. The sources publish different qualitative suitability guidance. (medium confidence)

CoinAPI's survivorship article describes a point-in-time universe as the tradable universe at the historical selection date, including markets that later become inactive or delisted and using information available by that date. Gimmer similarly recommends date-specific eligibility and retention of removed markets through the last eligible observation. (medium confidence)

Gimmer recommends applying liquidity, trading-history, price and other selection filters using information available at the selection timestamp, and warns that current market capitalization or present-day volume reintroduces future knowledge. CoinAPI likewise recommends a point-in-time universe and signals restricted to information available at that date. (medium confidence)

CoinAPI lists delisted pairs, changed symbol conventions, expired derivatives and venue shutdowns as sources of crypto survivorship bias. Gimmer separately warns against silently merging renamed assets and recommends verifying identity and conversion boundaries. (medium confidence)

Gimmer's proposed selection-log workflow records each rebalance timestamp and market identity, applies contemporaneous filters, classifies exclusion reasons, and freezes the eligible set before strategy tuning. It recommends labeling a survivor-only sensitivity check as using later survival knowledge. These are the article's methodological recommendations. (low confidence)

CoinAPI's survivorship article describes separate active-symbol and historical-symbol endpoints with pagination and proposes combining their lists with coverage timestamps for a historical-universe workflow. Its data_start/data_end glossary says those fields are dataset-coverage bounds, not authoritative listing/delisting dates or a guarantee of continuous observations; coverage can begin after listing or end before delisting. The glossary says active-symbol data_end can move and recommends recording the metadata snapshot timestamp. These are provider descriptions, without verified endpoint execution or a demonstrated complete historical venue universe. (low confidence)

Freqtrade's retrieved plugin documentation states that VolumePairList sorts by quoteVolume, normally using the exchange's last-24-hour ticker data, and does not support backtesting mode. A maintainer in a September 2022 issue separately stated that StaticPairList was enforced for backtesting at that time. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Freqtrade's retrieved documentation gives an AgeFilter minimum listing-age default of 10 days and a SpreadFilter max_spread_ratio default of 0.005. It states that DelistFilter removes scheduled delistings on supported exchanges and does not support backtesting mode. These are software defaults and support limits. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Gimmer states that its public Running Backtest guide does not establish that the public workflow reconstructs a point-in-time cryptocurrency universe or repairs delisted data; it describes universe construction as a separate research step. (low confidence)

Cong, Li, Tang and Yang classify three sampled exchanges with NYSDFS BitLicense as regulated and the other 26 as unregulated, and state that their reported empirical findings use the New York regulation standard unless otherwise specified. (low confidence)

CoinMarketCap distinguishes trading volume, which counts assets changing hands, from its liquidity measure. In their review of earlier wash-trading work, Cong, Li, Tang and Yang state that there is no theoretical underpinning for any particular link between slippage and total volume. (medium confidence)

Freqtrade documents that StaticPairList allows only currently enabled pairs by default, with allow_inactive=true available to skip active-market validation. Gimmer separately warns that using a current exchange directory for an earlier historical test uses later survival information; it recommends a separate eligibility record for each historical selection date. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)
FINRA and the SEC investor glossary define scheduled dollar-cost averaging as investing equal amounts at regular intervals regardless of market fluctuations. (medium confidence)

FINRA says a fixed investment schedule can reduce emotional or impulsive decisions. Vanguard describes cost averaging as potentially helping a loss-averse investor preserve commitment to an investment plan. (medium confidence)

Vanguard reports that lump-sum investment outperformed common cost-averaging strategies roughly two-thirds of the time in its historical and simulated analysis. Its cited historical context concerns stocks, bonds and cash; the result is not a crypto-coin selection backtest. (low confidence)
Vanguard cautions that past performance does not guarantee future returns and that index performance does not exactly represent an investable product. (low confidence)

Coinbase's fee disclosure states that simple buys include a spread, and that transaction fees can depend on payment method, order size, market conditions, location and asset, with fees shown in the trade preview. Kraken's disclosure separately states that recurring purchases include a spread and that payment fees can depend on payment method. These product-specific disclosures do not give one recurring-buy cost applicable to every account. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Zhang and Watts's HODL study data section starts from the top 800 CoinMarketCap assets and applies eligibility filters including removal of assets first observed on or after 2024-01-01, assets with low recent average volume, and assets whose latest observation predates 2025-04-26. Those filters define the universe for its reported results. (low confidence)

The GIPS Firms Handbook warns that annualizing a return from less than a year extrapolates the observed partial-period performance into a simulated annual result. It also warns that an annualized internal rate of return from a short-period calculation must be converted to a non-annualized result for that reporting context. Short bot trials should disclose the measurement period and avoid presenting extrapolated annual performance as a realized year. (low confidence)

Bailey and coauthors warn that standard holdout techniques can be unreliable in investment backtests and propose combinatorially symmetric cross-validation as a way to estimate probability of backtest overfitting. (low confidence)
Bailey and coauthors define probability of backtest overfitting as the conditional probability that a strategy selected as optimal in sample underperforms the median out of sample. (low confidence)

Quantpedia contrasts marking portfolio value through time with reporting only closed trades. In its daily-reset grid example, closed-trade reporting can show only winning trades during the day and hide losses until the remaining inventory closes. (low confidence)

Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin define Conditional Drawdown measures as functionals of a portfolio's drawdown or underwater curve. For a single path and an appropriate tolerance parameter, the drawdown functional is the mean of the worst tail of drawdowns. (low confidence)
Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin state that the Conditional Drawdown family includes maximum drawdown and average drawdown as limiting cases. (low confidence)

In their CSCV implementation, Bailey and coauthors require synchronous performance observations across candidate configurations and say that configurations trading at different frequencies should be aggregated to a common time index. They also require the selection metric to be estimable on subsamples of each candidate performance series. (low confidence)

The Frontiers crypto microstructure study explicitly states that its economic evaluation includes maker/taker fees and half-spread slippage but omits queue-position dynamics, perpetual-futures funding, short-borrow costs, and matching-engine latency. The authors therefore characterize its reported net Sharpe figures as an upper bound for a non-co-located retail-fee participant. (low confidence)

The abstract of Arian, Norouzi and Seco reports lower backtest-overfitting probability and a better Deflated Sharpe Ratio for CPCV than traditional methods, and reports shortcomings in false-discovery prevention for Walk-Forward. The abstract identifies a synthetic controlled environment with stochastic-volatility, jump-diffusion, drift-burst and regime-switching models. This is an attributed comparison reported in the publisher preview; it does not establish that CPCV universally dominates walk-forward validation for crypto grid/DCA selectors. (low confidence)
